title: Universal machines, halting, and Church's lambda calculus
text:
CHAPTER 3. TURING AND COMPUTABILITY
SECTION 3.2. UNIVERSAL MACHINES, HALTING, AND CHURCH'S LAMBDA CALCULUS

Section 3.1 described Turing machines and how Turing answered Hilbert. This section develops three ideas from the same body of work that matter most for engineers: the universal machine, which is the theoretical blueprint of the stored-program computer; the halting problem, the modern textbook form of undecidability; and lambda calculus, the other 1936 model of computation, which shaped AI programming languages.

1. The universal machine

In the 1936 paper Turing showed that there is a single machine U which, given on its tape the standard description of any machine M followed by an input, will carry out exactly what M would do on that input. U is the universal machine.

How can a fixed, finite table imitate any other table? The key is that M's table is just a string of symbols on U's tape. U's own rules implement an interpreter loop, which in modern pseudocode looks like this:

    tape contains: [description of M] [marker] [simulated tape of M, with M's current state and head position marked]
    loop:
        find M's current state and the symbol under M's simulated head
        search M's description for the matching rule (state, symbol)
        if no rule: halt
        write the new symbol on the simulated tape
        move the simulated head marker left or right
        record the new state
    repeat

Every step of M costs U many steps of shuttling back and forth across the tape, so U is slow, but it is exact. Turing's original construction contained some errors, later pointed out (notably by Emil Post in 1947) and fixed, but the idea was sound.

Why the universal machine matters for engineering. Before about 1945, a computing machine was built or configured for a class of jobs: ENIAC (Section 4.3) was reprogrammed by plugging cables. The universal machine says that one fixed piece of hardware, given the right description as data, can do any computation. That is precisely what a modern CPU is: a fixed circuit that fetches instructions from memory and interprets them. The "fetch, decode, execute" cycle is U's loop implemented in silicon. Whether, and how much, the designers of the first stored-program computers were directly influenced by Turing's paper is debated among historians. John von Neumann knew Turing's work, and Turing himself designed a stored-program computer, the ACE, in 1945-1946 (Section 4.4). The conceptual link is clear even where the historical influence is debated.

Software interpreters and emulators are universal machines too. A Python interpreter, the Java virtual machine, and an emulator running an old game console on your laptop are all programs that take another program as data and carry out its behavior.

How small can a universal machine be? Researchers have found universal Turing machines with only a handful of states and symbols. Claude Shannon showed in 1956 that a universal machine needs only two states if it may use many symbols, or two symbols if it may use many states. Marvin Minsky found a small universal machine in 1962 with 7 states and 4 symbols. The precise records have changed over time; the point is that universality needs remarkably little hardware.

2. Turing completeness

A system is called Turing complete if it can simulate any Turing machine (given unbounded memory). Almost every programming language is Turing complete, as are many things that were not designed as computers: Conway's Game of Life cellular automaton, certain card games under particular rules, spreadsheet formulas in some versions, and even some instruction subsets of real processors. Roughly speaking, you need:

  - a way to store and retrieve an unbounded amount of data (or at least as much as you need);
  - conditional behavior (do this or that depending on data);
  - repetition (loops or recursion).

This is why the conditional branch is so important in the history of hardware (Sections 1.3, 2.3, 2.4). The Z3 and the Harvard Mark I in their original form lacked it, so their practical programming model was not Turing complete, even if clever theoretical constructions can recover universality.

Real computers have finite memory, so strictly speaking they are enormous finite-state machines. Engineers still treat them as Turing complete because their memory is large enough that the difference rarely matters, and because memory can be extended.

3. The halting problem

The textbook form of Turing's result is the halting problem: is there a program HALTS(P, x) that, for every program P and input x, returns true if P eventually stops when run on x and false if it runs forever?

The answer is no. Proof by contradiction, in pseudocode:

    Suppose HALTS(P, x) exists and always answers correctly.
    Define a new program:

    TROUBLE(P):
        if HALTS(P, P):      -- would P halt when given its own code as input?
            loop forever
        else:
            halt

    Now ask: does TROUBLE(TROUBLE) halt?
      If HALTS(TROUBLE, TROUBLE) is true, TROUBLE loops forever: contradiction.
      If it is false, TROUBLE halts: contradiction.
    Therefore HALTS cannot exist.

This proof uses the same two ingredients as Goedel and Turing: programs as data (P can be passed its own code), and diagonalization (feed the construction to itself). The formulation in terms of "halting" is not word for word in Turing's 1936 paper, which, as Section 3.1 explained, talked about circle-free machines and about whether a machine ever prints a given symbol. The halting form became standard through later textbooks; the logician Martin Davis is often credited with popularizing the term in the 1950s. Turing's results are equivalent in substance, which is why the halting problem is routinely credited to him.

What the halting problem does and does not say:

  - It does NOT say you can never tell whether a particular program halts. For most programs you write, you can. It says no single algorithm works for all programs.
  - It does not depend on hardware. It holds for any Turing-complete system.
  - Many other problems are undecidable because the halting problem could be reduced to them. Rice's theorem (Henry Gordon Rice, 1953) states that every nontrivial property of the function a program computes is undecidable. Will the program ever output a password? Does it compute the same function as another program? Undecidable in general.

Practical consequences: static analyzers, compilers and verification tools must either be incomplete (sometimes answer "don't know"), unsound (sometimes wrong), or restricted to limited classes of programs. Safety-critical embedded software, such as code you may write for automotive or aerospace controllers, is often written in restricted styles (bounded loops, no recursion, static memory) precisely so that properties such as termination and maximum execution time can be checked.

4. The busy beaver: undecidability you can feel

The busy beaver function, introduced by Tibor Rado in 1962, makes the halting problem concrete. Consider all Turing machines with n states and two symbols (0 and 1) that start on a blank tape and eventually halt. BB(n) is the maximum number of steps any of them takes before halting (definitions vary slightly; some use the number of 1s left on the tape).

BB(n) grows faster than any computable function, because if you could compute an upper bound on BB(n), you could solve the halting problem for n-state machines: just run each machine for that many steps, and any machine still running will never halt.

Known values are tiny for small n and then explode. For two-symbol machines, the maximum step counts are 1, 6, 21 and 107 for n = 1 to 4. In 2024 a collaborative online project, the Busy Beaver Challenge, completed a computer-verified proof that BB(5) = 47,176,870 steps. BB(6) is known to be astronomically larger, and researchers have shown that the value of BB(n) for some modestly sized n (a few hundred states) cannot be proven within standard set theory at all. A few hundred states is less than many simple embedded controllers. The boundary of the knowable is closer than it looks.

5. Lambda calculus in a little more depth

Church's lambda calculus has just three kinds of expressions:

    variables:     x
    abstraction:   \x. M          (a function with parameter x and body M)
    application:   M N            (apply function M to argument N)

and one main computation rule, beta reduction:

    (\x. M) N   ->   M with every free x replaced by N

Example: (\x. x + 1) 4 -> 4 + 1. (Pure lambda calculus has no built-in "+" or "4"; everything must be encoded as functions. We use them here just to show the shape of a reduction.)

Encoding data as functions. Church numerals represent the number n as "apply a function f to x, n times":

    0 = \f. \x. x
    1 = \f. \x. f x
    2 = \f. \x. f (f x)
    3 = \f. \x. f (f (f x))

    SUCC = \n. \f. \x. f (n f x)          (add one more application of f)
    PLUS = \m. \n. \f. \x. m f (n f x)

Booleans can be encoded as choosers:

    TRUE  = \a. \b. a
    FALSE = \a. \b. b
    IF c THEN p ELSE q  =  c p q

So a boolean is literally a function that selects one of two branches. Compare this with Boole's 0/1 algebra (Section 1.1) and with relay contacts selecting a path (Section 2.1): very different notations for the same notion of a binary choice.

Recursion without names. Lambda calculus has no loops and no named functions, yet it can express recursion through a fixed-point combinator, the best known being the Y combinator, attributed to Haskell Curry:

    Y = \f. (\x. f (x x)) (\x. f (x x))

It satisfies Y g = g (Y g), so Y g behaves like a function that can call itself. That self-application (x x) is the lambda-calculus version of a program being fed its own code, the same trick that powers the diagonal arguments above.

Equivalence and undecidability. Church proved that there is no lambda expression that decides whether two arbitrary lambda expressions are equivalent (reduce to the same normal form), and used this to show the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable. As noted in Section 3.1, Turing proved his machines and lambda calculus compute exactly the same functions.

6. Two styles of computing, two styles of AI programming

The Turing machine and lambda calculus represent two styles that recur throughout computing:

  Imperative / machine style: a state that is modified step by step (tape, registers, memory). This matches hardware directly and leads to assembly language, FORTRAN, C, and the von Neumann architecture.

  Functional / expression style: computation as evaluating expressions and applying functions, with no explicit mutable state. This leads to LISP (1958), ML, Haskell and the functional parts of modern languages.

Early AI chose the functional style in LISP (Section 9.2) because AI programs manipulated symbolic expressions (formulas, lists, trees), and LISP made it natural to treat programs themselves as data, which was useful for programs that reason about or generate other programs. Modern deep learning frameworks, interestingly, have come back to functional ideas: libraries such as JAX transform pure functions (for example, automatically computing gradients), while hardware remains imperative underneath.

7. Computability versus feasibility

Computability theory asks what can be computed at all, with unlimited time and memory. An engineer must also ask what can be computed in a reasonable time. A problem may be decidable but take longer than the age of the universe for realistic inputs. That is the domain of complexity theory, developed from the 1960s (Hartmanis and Stearns, 1965, are usually credited with founding the field) and given its central open question, whether P equals NP, by Cook (1971) and Karp (1972). Much of AI history is about problems that are computable but infeasible to solve exactly, such as finding the best chess move by exhaustive search or the optimal plan for a robot, and about the heuristics, approximations and learning methods developed to cope.

8. Summary

  - Turing's universal machine U interprets the description of any machine M given as data; it is the theoretical model of the stored-program computer and of every interpreter and emulator.
  - Turing completeness needs unbounded storage, conditional behavior and repetition; it is surprisingly easy to achieve.
  - The halting problem (no program can decide for all programs and inputs whether they halt) is the modern form of Turing's 1936 undecidability result; Rice's theorem extends it to all nontrivial behavioral properties.
  - The busy beaver function grows faster than any computable function; BB(5) = 47,176,870 was proved in 2024.
  - Lambda calculus models computation by function application and substitution, encodes numbers and booleans as functions, achieves recursion through fixed-point combinators, and inspired LISP.
